clue.text: Labour follower: “Half of London is a corrupt place”

indicators.note: half of a word means only one of its two halves is kept, here the front portion

blocks.note: what follows labour in childbirth is the newborn
a letter selection: the first three of its six letters, one half

explanation.surface: A Labour party supporter quoted complaining that half of the capital is rotten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' with a capital L looks political, but it is childbirth, and what comes after labour is a baby.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient city became a byword, from the Bible onward, for any decadent, sinful metropolis.

clue.text: Mark from Flanders leaving France for Britain

indicators.note: quitting one country for another swaps one abbreviation out and puts the other in its place

blocks.note: the adjective for the region of Belgium
F is the international code for France
B is a standard abbreviation for Britain or British

explanation.surface: Someone tracing a mark of origin as it moves from Flanders over to Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: The F of FLEMISH is the letter for France; replace it with B for Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A blemish is a spot, stain or flaw on a surface, which is exactly what a mark can be.

clue.text: A worker present ultimately during boozy sesh

definitions.text: A worker present ultimately during boozy sesh

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the closing letter of each word is taken
something happening during an event sits inside its span, so these letters go within the others

blocks.note: a bender is a drinking spree
the final letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A worker who stays to the very end of a drinking session.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: read as wordplay it builds the word, read plainly it describes the person serving at the drinking spree. A bender is slang for a heavy drinking bout.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone employed behind the bar is necessarily there throughout every boozy session, pouring the drinks until closing.

clue.text: Tree line eventually hides unit attacking at front

indicators.note: read as going from start to eventual finish, so the opening and closing letters are kept
at the front means the leading letter of each word is the one that counts

blocks.note: its first and last letters
the initials of the three words

explanation.surface: A military unit hiding along a tree line before attacking from the front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hides' looks like a container signal but is simply one of the words giving its initial letter. The lehua is an obscure Hawaiian flowering tree, worth checking against crossers.
explanation.definitionFit: The lehua, or ohia lehua, is a Hawaiian evergreen with red bottlebrush flowers, so it is one particular species of tree.

clue.text: Silly trick in PE leaves one in critical condition

indicators.note: something silly is nonsensical, so the letters are muddled into a new order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A daft stunt in a school gym class lands a pupil in hospital in a critical state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Critical condition' reads as a medical emergency, but it means a fault-finding frame of mind. PE is physical education, a school gym lesson.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedant who fusses over tiny faults is always in a mood of criticism, a playful reading of a hospital phrase.

clue.text: Can of fizzy cocktail

blocks.note: first meaning: slang for prison
second meaning: a tequila drink mixed with a fizzy mixer and banged on the bar

explanation.surface: Someone asking for a tin of a sparkling mixed drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' reads as a drinks tin but is the slang for jail. A tequila slammer is topped with lemonade or sparkling wine and slammed down to make it fizz.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are slang: jail is called the can, and the bar drink takes its name from being banged on the counter.

clue.text: Boy seen around a large Barnet establishment?

indicators.note: to be seen around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses the rest

blocks.note: a boy is a son
taken as written
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A boy spotted hanging around a big business in the north London district of Barnet.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnet looks like the London borough, but it is rhyming slang: Barnet Fair means hair. The question mark flags this playful sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairdressing business is called a salon, so in rhyming slang it is a place dealing with your barnet.

clue.text: A reverberating of bells on radio is pleasing

indicators.note: on the radio things are heard rather than seen, so only the sound matters

blocks.note: a pealing is a ringing of bells

explanation.surface: A broadcast of church bells ringing out makes pleasant listening.
explanation.walkthrough: A peal is a full ringing of church bells; said as one phrase, A PEALING sounds just like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something attractive or agreeable is appealing, a straightforward synonym of pleasing as an adjective.

clue.text: French underground force soldiers repelled

indicators.note: something repelled is driven back, so these letters run in the backward direction

blocks.note: the Met is London's Metropolitan Police force
OR is other ranks, ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: The French Resistance beating back occupying troops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French underground force' paints the wartime Resistance, but the definition is just the first two words. The Met is London's police force.
explanation.definitionFit: The Paris subway system is the Métro, so the city's underground railway is literally called this name.

clue.text: Being extra-playful when topless is more perilous

indicators.note: without a top means the head is gone, so the first letter is dropped

blocks.note: frisky means playful, and this is the comparative

explanation.surface: Getting extra frisky without your top on is a more dangerous game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' looks like nudity but just removes the first letter of a word down the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Riskier is the comparative of risky, meaning carrying greater danger, which matches perilous made comparative.

clue.text: Want to bump off daughter ... what are you on?

indicators.note: to bump off is to kill or get rid of, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: a dearth is a want or lack
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: Someone wanting to murder their daughter, met with a startled 'what are you on?'
explanation.walkthrough: 'What are you on?' reads as asking about drugs, but literally the thing we all stand on is the planet.
explanation.definitionFit: Everyone lives and stands upon the planet, so the cheeky question has the world beneath us as its literal reply.

clue.text: Those in two minds about ultimately clumsy heel taps

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the preceding word counts
a clumsy arrangement is a botched one, so the letters get jumbled

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Indecisive people fretting over awkward tapping heels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In two minds' usually means undecided; here it describes people who read thoughts, present in their own mind and another's.
explanation.definitionFit: Mind-readers supposedly share thoughts with someone else, so they are effectively inside two heads at once.

clue.text: Sex drug helping to get a repeated performance

blocks.note: IT is a crossword euphemism for sex
E is ecstasy
a ration is a helping or portion

explanation.surface: A pill that boosts sexual stamina for a second round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Helping' looks like a verb meaning aiding, but it is a noun: a portion.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something again and again, as with a repeated procedure or another run-through, is an iteration.

clue.text: A drop of IPA and I look around for a saucy type

indicators.note: a drop is a tiny amount, so only the leading letter of the word is used
turning around faces the other way, so the letters run backward

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of the beer
taken as written
lo is an old word for look

explanation.surface: A sip of pale ale, then a glance around the bar for a cheeky character.
explanation.walkthrough: IPA is India pale ale, a beer. 'Saucy type' sounds like a flirt, but it is a kind of sauce; lo means look, as in lo and behold.
explanation.definitionFit: The garlic mayonnaise from Provence is one particular variety of sauce, hence a playful saucy sort.

clue.text: Headless disembodied souls in hell

indicators.note: without a head means the first letter has been cut away

blocks.note: shades are ghosts or spirits of the dead

explanation.surface: Decapitated ghosts drifting through the underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: Shades is the classical word for the spirits of the dead, which fits the underworld picture neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the underworld realm of the dead is called by this name, used loosely as a word for the inferno.

clue.text: Soprano taking time out in old foreign capital

blocks.note: S is the musical abbreviation for soprano
chilling is slang for relaxing

explanation.surface: An opera singer enjoying a break in a historic overseas city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' suggests a city, but here it means money: the old currency of Austria before the euro.
explanation.definitionFit: The schilling was Austria's currency until the euro replaced it, so it is former money from abroad, capital in the financial sense.

clue.text: Nixon aide stealing a dollar from Paul Stanley?

indicators.note: stealing something takes it away, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: he is the singer of the rock band Kiss
the dollar sign looks like an S

explanation.surface: A Watergate-era White House staffer pinching a buck from a rock star.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul Stanley fronts the band Kiss, so he is a Kiss singer; one of the three adjacent S letters is taken away.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Kissinger served Richard Nixon as National Security Advisor and Secretary of State.

clue.text: He parades around foremost of army units

indicators.note: moved around means shuffled out of place, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: An officer marching about at the head of his troops.
explanation.walkthrough: The parade picture suits the army, but the words he parades are simply the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The leading force of an attack is called its spearhead, the unit out in front of the rest.

clue.text: One who fought a dog trial unrestrainedly

indicators.note: without restraint the letters run loose and land in a new order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who wrestled wildly with a dog during an obedience competition.
explanation.walkthrough: A dog trial is a sheepdog or obedience contest; the phrase is just the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Roman arena combatants battled each other or beasts for public entertainment, so such a person fought.

clue.text: One drawing loads of craft in cold bay, say

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: C is the tap abbreviation for cold
art is a craft or skill
a bay is a brown horse; 'say' marks it as an example

explanation.surface: Someone sketching lots of boats moored in a chilly inlet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawing' and 'craft' suggest sketching boats, but drawing means pulling and bay is a horse colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy draught animal pulls wagons, so it is literally a creature that hauls burdens.

clue.text: Success pitilessly stymies one full of crap

indicators.note: to stymie is to block or hem in, so the words hold the answer trapped inside them

blocks.note: runs across the two words

explanation.surface: Ruthless success thwarts someone who talks nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One full of crap' sounds like a bluffer, but taken literally it is a pit for sewage.
explanation.definitionFit: A pit for collecting sewage and waste is literally a receptacle filled with excrement.

clue.text: Understand German? Speak with harsh and grating tone!

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for German

blocks.clueFragment: Speak with harsh and grating tone
blocks.note: to rasp is to speak harshly

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone can follow German, then telling them to speak it gutturally.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface plays on the stereotype of German sounding harsh; 'German' gives a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To get your head around an idea is to comprehend it, a common figurative use of seizing with the hand.

clue.text: Moneypenny is one first to notice Bond's undies

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, which is all that is kept

blocks.note: Miss Moneypenny is M's personal assistant in the James Bond stories
its opening letter
ties are bonds

explanation.surface: M's secretary is the first to spot 007's underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bond's' reads as James Bond's, but it means bonds, i.e. ties. PA is a personal assistant.
explanation.definitionFit: Knickers are a type of underwear, and undies is the informal word for underwear generally.

clue.text: Cause damage to 9 houses close to Sidcup

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only the last letter is taken
a house holds things inside it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: the answer to 9 across is a synonym of soil
its final letter

explanation.surface: Vandalising homes near Sidcup, a suburb in south-east London.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference '9' means the answer to 9 across, which must be swapped for a synonym, soil, before it can enclose anything.
explanation.definitionFit: To ruin or impair something is to spoil it, a direct verb synonym for harming it.

clue.text: I love to gyrate around fellow from Muscat

indicators.note: spinning round turns the letters to face the other way
going around something surrounds it, so the other piece sits inside

blocks.note: taken as written
love is zero, the letter O
a fellow is a man

explanation.surface: A confession of enjoying dancing around a man from the Gulf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fellow from Muscat' looks like the definition, but 'fellow' is needed for letters; the definition is just 'from Muscat'.
explanation.definitionFit: Muscat is the capital of Oman, so anything originating there is described by the national adjective.

clue.text: Islander jiggled about in a bad bra

indicators.note: things jiggled about are shaken loose, so the letters fall into a different order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A Caribbean resident bouncing around in an ill-fitting bra.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder sits right after the indicator, and every letter of the bad bra is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone native to Barbados lives on a Caribbean island, so they are a person from an island.

clue.text: Obscure cut by European is more melancholy

indicators.note: something cut by another thing has that thing driven into it, so a piece goes inside

blocks.note: to blur is to obscure
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: An unknown person snubbed by a fellow European feels sadder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obscure' reads as an adjective but is the verb blur; 'cut by' means the E is inserted into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling blue means being sad, so the comparative describes someone sadder or gloomier.

clue.text: Carry On performers perhaps appearing in court

blocks.note: a group of performers can be an act, as in a double act
a defendant is up before the magistrate

explanation.surface: Stars of the British Carry On comedy films turning up in a courtroom.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make 'Carry On' look like the British film series of bawdy comedies, but as a definition it is the phrasal verb to carry on, meaning misbehave.
explanation.definitionFit: To carry on is to make a fuss or behave badly, which is exactly what children do when they act up.

clue.text: "Freedom requires power first" is a trite remark

indicators.note: coming first means going at the very front of the assembled word

blocks.note: P is the abbreviation for power
latitude is freedom of action

explanation.surface: A slogan about liberty depending on power, dismissed as a cliché.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted saying is itself the sort of hollow line the answer describes.
explanation.definitionFit: A platitude is a dull, overused statement offered as if it were profound, so it is a hackneyed comment.

clue.text: African expression of disapproval one's rebuffed

indicators.note: something rebuffed is pushed back, so the letters run backward

blocks.note: tut is the clicking sound of disapproval
one is I, and 's is is

explanation.surface: An African tutting because their advances were rejected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' splits as I (one) plus the contraction of is.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tutsi are a people of Rwanda and Burundi, so a member is a particular kind of person from that continent.

clue.text: Provoke first of revellers to punch bouncer?

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter alone
a punch goes into its target, so one piece is driven inside another

blocks.note: the bouncing tiger from Winnie-the-Pooh
its opening letter

explanation.surface: A rowdy partygoer goads a nightclub doorman into a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bouncer' looks like a doorman, but the question mark points to Tigger, the bouncy tiger in Winnie-the-Pooh.
explanation.definitionFit: To set off a reaction or spark a response is to provoke it, a common verb synonym.

clue.text: Bed-bound types holding record for splits

indicators.note: holding something keeps it inside, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: darts are thrown at the double and treble beds on a board
an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: Invalids confined to bed who still hold the world record for doing the splits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bed-bound' suggests the sick, but in darts the segments of the board are called beds, so darts are heading for beds.
explanation.definitionFit: Splits is slang for leaves or goes away, which is what someone does when they set off.
